newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Jail beckons for S.Korean president's son.
newsitem.headline: Jail beckons for S.Korean president's son.

text.p: A South Korean court issued an arrest warrant on Saturday for President Kim Young-sam's son on charges of taking bribes worth millions of dollars and evading taxes.
State prosecutors had sought the arrest of the junior Kim for taking kickbacks of 3.2 billion won ($3.6 million) in return for business favours to alumni of his old high school.
He has denied accepting bribes.
Kim Hyun-chul, dubbed the "crown prince" by the media, is also accused of evading taxes on 3.3 billion won given to him by businessmen, but not as bribes, a prosecution official said.
An arrest would bring to a climax a corruption scandal involving top politicians, bankers and businessmen that emerged from the rubble of the country's largest ever bankruptcy in January.
If convicted of bribery, Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, faces a maximum sentence of five years in jail.

Public attention is now riveted on President Kim, who has been badly wounded by the scandal stemming from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co under five trillion won of debts acquired by string-pulling in high places.
The president, who was swept to power on an anti-graft ticket, is expected to issue an apology.
Kim Hyun-chul would be the first child of a serving South Korean head of state to be jailed.

The Korea Herald newspaper on Saturday quoted justice ministry officials as saying he would most likely end up in a detention centre in the southern suburbs of Seoul where former president Roh Tae-woo is being held.
"Though he is the son of the incubent president, he will be treated in the same manner as other common inmates," a ministry official was quoted as saying.
Roh is serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and other crimes. His predecessor, Chun Doo Hwan, is serving a life sentence in another prison on similar charges.
Kim Hyun-chul was summoned by state prosecutors for questioning on Thursday and has been at the Supreme Public Prosecutors' Office ever since.
The charges do not relate directly to Hanbo's failure, which sparked a wide-ranging prosecution graft enquiry that eventually snared the president's son.
Prosecutors had been trying to dig up evidence that Kim Hyun-chul used his influence to obtain lucrative broadcasting, cable television and telecommunications licences for his associates.
In addition, they were looking into allegations that he laundered through companies owned by his cronies as much as 10 billion won of unspent funds from his father's 1992 election campaign.
The election slush funds have become a hot political issue for his father, who is under growing public pressure to make a full accounting of his 1992 campaign finances.
Media reports said Kim Hyun-chul wrote a letter to a friend before being summoned vowing to "use all means at my disposal to fight any legal prosecution, including arrest".
"I will wage this fight not as the son of the president but as Hyun-chul, an individual," the letter was quoted as saying.

Officials at the presidential Blue House, anxious to put the scandal behind them, were clearly stunned. "It is a mere expression of an emotional young man's feelings," the Korean Times quoted one presidential aide as saying.
Opposition parties have alleged that Hanbo Steel received preferential loans as a reward for donations of up to 90 billion won to Kim Young-sam's election campaign, which his son helped to manage.
Eleven people, including three of President Kim's top aides, are standing trial over the Hanbo scandal.
